giai_trinh.T05: Điểm mở phần 'Chuyển giao' của trục kể do chủ dự án duyệt ở G1: lời mở đầu đoạn 05 là 'Then came the second kind of work', nên hình đổi chủ ý từ phòng tính toán sang phòng máy rơ-le 1947 (nơi xuất hiện công việc thứ hai), có tiếng rơ-le vào trước hình 0,5 s và phụ đề 'the second kind of work' ngay chữ 'second'. Ngay sau đó là ảnh NASA 1947 của chính phòng máy Bell, nên người xem được neo nơi chốn trong vòng 4 s.
giai_trinh.T09: Cầu nối có chủ ý của kịch bản khoá (đoạn 09: 'The lamplighter walks on'), chuyển từ quá khứ sang hiện tại theo ẩn dụ ngọn lửa trao tay mà chủ dự án đặt cho kênh: J-cut tiếng bước chân người thắp đèn vào trước hình 1,2 s, cùng dải cửa sổ phòng tính toán tắt rồi một tầng tháp bừng sáng. Một người xem không nêu điểm này.
giai_trinh.T15: Match cut có chủ ý của kịch bản khoá: ngọn đèn trên đầu thang (câu hỏi 'where will the next beginners learn?') khớp với ngọn đèn khí cạnh dải cửa sổ ở đoạn Kết; câu móc 'What happens to a job when a machine takes its name?' lặp lại nguyên văn câu mở đầu phim để đóng vòng kể (Mở + Kết theo CHUAN-KENH §2). Một người xem không nêu điểm này.

R1.question: When a machine takes over the work a job is named for, as with human computers, programmers and now AI-assisted coders, does the work disappear or move on, and can the newest workers move on with it?

issues.note: After the 1990 handbook quote card about AI as just additional tools, the film cuts abruptly to the lamplighter street scene. The link between the lamplighter metaphor and the quote is not made visually or in the narration, so the jump feels unmotivated.

The film cuts from a dark ladder and lamp abstraction to the bright dusk street. The ladder and lamp symbolism for beginners learning is not explained, so the images do not clearly match the narration.
Quote cards (R11.1 to R11.3) hold the same text-only page for about 12 s with little new to look at.
Frames R12.5 to R12.8 stay on the same desk and monitor close-up while the text changes. The picture barely changes for about 16 s.
The same dark empty-office view stays on screen through the Stanford section (R14.6 to R14.8). Nothing new appears except captions.
The same dark office stays on screen from R15.6 through R16.3, about 28 s, with only caption changes.

R2.question: When a machine takes over a job's name and its routine tasks, as computers did to human computers and programmers, can the newest workers still find a way to learn and move on to the work that remains?

issues.note: The cut from the warm interior of the computing room to a dusk street with a lamplighter has a lower-third caption ('same word - three different jobs') that disappears abruptly. The lamplighter figure is a tiny silhouette and the link between lamplighter and computer is not yet clear.

The jump from the 1950s office to a dark, empty archive corridor for 'the second kind of work' has no visual hook. The caption flickers in only at +2.5 s, and the corridor does not obviously show programming.

The narration says 'two job titles' while the picture is still the single programmer desk with the 'computer programmers' label. The second title, software developers, comes later at T12, so the picture lags the narration.

The split-screen (Langley 1940s / today) reuses the desk imagery to say 'checking the machine's numbers: an old job here'. It then cuts to a dim, wide, empty office for 'the people just starting out', and that shot does not show beginners.

After the ladder and dark-floor shot for 'where will the next beginners learn?', the film jumps straight to the dusk street. The caption 'What happens to a job when a machine takes its name?' is a new question that is not tied to the preceding thought.

The 'Women computers at the Langley laboratory' pictogram chart (75 women) sits abruptly between a historical photo and a 3D office, and its figures are small. It is a style break from the rest of the film.
The BLS quote card sits on screen for about 8 s, and the text hardly changes between the two frames.
The card with 'Programming is one of many work activities...' stays up for roughly 8 to 12 s over several frames, with little new to look at.
The dim, empty office is reused many times in the section on young workers (R15.6 to R17.2, R17.3 to R17.4), so the picture hardly changes across a long stretch of statistics narration.
The same dim open-plan office angle repeats across R16.5 to R17.4 while the captions change but the picture does not.

R3.question: When a machine takes over the routine part of a job that carries a name (human computer, programmer), do people move on to new work, and can the newest workers still get in and learn?

issues.note: Hard cut from the dusk street and lamplighter into a close desk with a typewriter. The caption bridges it, but the narration starts a new idea with no visual link.
The bright, integrated classroom cuts to a dark archive corridor with no establishing link. 'The second kind of work' is not shown as a change of place or time, and the look changes a lot.
The jump to the 'today' night office is abrupt. The lamplighter motif has gone and the look is cold blue, so the new setting is not introduced for a while.
The same dark ladder-and-lamp picture holds for about 16 seconds (R13.1 to R13.4) while the stats change on screen. There is little new to look at.
The same empty night office is reused for several consecutive frames (R12.6, R12.7 and again in R14). The images are static and repetitive while the narration stays abstract.
The camera stays on the programmer's screen for a long stretch (R11.4 to R11.5, R12.4 to R12.5, R12.8) with only the text changing.
Quote cards on a flat background are shown twice in a row (R10.5 to R10.6, then R11.1 to R11.3). They are text-heavy and visually static.
